sections.h2: Recording a deed in Apache County
sections.html:
The County Recorder in St. Johns, the county seat, records deeds for Apache County property. You will find the office at 75 West Cleveland, PO Box 425, St. Johns, AZ 85936. The phone is 928-337-7515, the fax is 928-337-7676, and recording questions can go to recordings@co.apache.az.us.

  • The counter opens at 6:30 a.m. and closes at 5:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday.
  • The archive reaches back to 1879.
  • Each recorded document is treated as an original, kept and indexed by the office, and open for the public to view.

With the counter closed Friday through Sunday, an in-person recording has to be planned around the Monday to Thursday window. A title or escrow company records most sales, so many owners never go in at all. If you are handling a family or inherited transfer on your own, phone ahead and ask what the office will require.

sections.h2: Forms and tools from the Recorder
sections.html:
Besides documents, the Recorder handles voter registration and early ballots, though only the document side concerns a seller. Several resources are worth collecting before you file anything:

  • A cover sheet for recordings.
  • A summary of the recording requirements in A.R.S. 11-480.
  • An account application for frequent filers.
  • An empty affidavit of property value.
  • Guides on homestead exemptions and on property transfers.
  • A search tool for recorded documents.

Try the search tool on your own deed and on any recorded liens before listing. You will be looking at the same record a title company reviews, so any problem comes to light while there is still time to fix it.

The base fee under A.R.S. 11-475 is $30 per instrument for most papers.

ServiceFee
Recording most papers required or authorized by law$30 per instrument
Recording for the U.S., the state or a political subdivision at its own request$15 per instrument
Copies of a record$1 per page or partial page
Recorder's certificate and seal on a copy$3 extra

Section 11-475.01 charges are already folded into the recording fees. Ask the office about copy pricing and extra charges before you write a check.

A deed or sales contract cannot be recorded in Arizona without an affidavit of legal value, which the county calls the affidavit of property value. Under A.R.S. 11-1133 the buyer and seller, or someone acting for either, swear to the facts on a Department of Revenue form.

Expect to supply quite a bit:

  • Contact details for both parties, plus an address for the tax statement.
  • The legal description and the street address, if there is one.
  • The closing date, the full price, the cash down payment and how the purchase was financed.
  • Whether furniture, equipment or other personal property worth 5% or more of the price was included.
  • The assessor's parcel number, any special terms, and whether the house will be lived in by the owner or rented out.

If anything is blank, the recorder has to turn the deed away unless it carries a note claiming an exemption under A.R.S. 11-1134. Marking an item not applicable counts as answering it.

Some transfers need no affidavit, but the deed must say which exemption applies, right on its face. A.R.S. 11-1134 sets the list. In plain terms it covers:

  • Gifts, and no-money quitclaim deeds that clear up title.
  • Transfers ordered by a court, and deeds that arise from partition.
  • Trustee's deeds after a power-of-sale foreclosure, and papers that only release a debt or pledge property as security for one.
  • Corrective or confirming deeds that restate an earlier recorded deed.
  • Residential transfers for token payment among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings.
  • Token-payment moves into or out of a trust, including a beneficiary deed.
  • Deeds issued after a delinquent-tax sale.

An ordinary arm's-length sale is not on that list, so a regular cash purchase comes with the completed affidavit. Unsure where your deed lands? An Arizona title company or attorney can tell you.

Apache County's Treasurer is also the public trustee, which is why deeds of trust name the Treasurer as trustee. That office can conduct trustee sales, issue certificates of purchase and redemption, issue trustee's deeds, and release a deed of trust at the lender's request.

If you are selling a house that still has a loan, this is the step to watch. The lender asks for a release after the payoff at closing, and the Recorder files it. Without a recorded release, the next sale of the property can stall, so make sure your payoff led to one.

You can find the Treasurer in the Recorder's building, at 75 West Cleveland in St. Johns, on the same four-day schedule.

sections.h2: If the Recorder turns a document away
sections.html:
A rejected recording is almost always a paperwork gap rather than a title problem. An incomplete affidavit, a missing exemption note or an unpaid fee will each stop a deed at the counter. Call 928-337-7515, ask exactly what is missing, fix it, and resubmit. Because the office is closed Fridays, a deed that bounces on Thursday afternoon waits until the next Monday, so aim to record earlier in the week when a closing date matters.

Sellers who work with a title company rarely see this, since the company checks the package first. If you are recording something yourself, such as a gift deed to a relative, read the exemption list above and write the exemption on the deed before you go.

Rural Apache County fills the northeast corner of Arizona. St. Johns is the seat and Eagar the largest town. Indian reservations, among them the Navajo Nation, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation and the Zuni Indian Reservation, cover 68.34 percent of the land. The 2020 count showed 28,723 housing units, of which 23.0% sat vacant, and owners lived in 73.2% of the occupied ones.

A parcel on or near reservation land, or on possessory rights land, deserves a call to the County Assessor, because improvements on possessory rights are counted as real property. Districts include St. Johns Unified, Round Valley Unified, Window Rock Unified, Chinle Unified and Ganado Unified, so check which one covers your address.

sections.h2: What a seller should have ready
sections.html:
The checklist is the same with or without a title company.

  1. Your current deed, showing the legal description and parcel number.
  2. A loan payoff figure, if a loan exists, and a plan for releasing the deed of trust.
  3. A finished affidavit, or the exemption your deed will name.
  4. Funds for the recording fees.
  5. A phone number for the buyer or the buyer's agent.

With cash there is no lender appraisal or underwriting, so this list is often everything. The title company files the deed, and a copy reaches you once the Recorder has processed it.

faqs.q: Where is the Apache County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: 75 West Cleveland, St. Johns, Arizona 85936. The counter is open Monday through Thursday, 6:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and the phone is 928-337-7515.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Apache County?
faqs.a: Most papers cost $30 per instrument. Copies run $1 per page, with $3 more for the recorder's certificate and seal. Check current charges with the office before mailing a check.

faqs.q: Does an Apache County sale need an affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: Yes, unless the deed names an exemption. Arizona requires a complete affidavit from the buyer and seller or their agents, and the recorder has to refuse a deed that lacks one.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed of gift to a family member in Apache County?
faqs.a: Yes, a gift deed is exempt, as are token-payment residential transfers among close relatives. The deed itself has to state the exemption.

faqs.q: Who releases a deed of trust in Apache County?
faqs.a: The Treasurer, who serves as public trustee, can release it once the lender asks. The release is then filed with the County Recorder.
